claims.evidence: This is a summary of the model's main finding with reference to figure

claims.claim: In rich media, the proteome efficiency of fermentation increases more rapidly and surpasses that of respiration, leading the cell to adopt fermentation as the optimal growth strategy.
claims.source: In rich media, however, the proteome efficiency of fermentation increases more rapidly and surpasses that of respiration (see Figure 1E), leading the cell to adopt fermentation as the optimal growth strategy.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the model's main finding with reference to figure

claims.claim: The model quantitatively illustrates the threshold-analog response in overflow metabolism when combined with cell heterogeneity.
claims.source: In further combination with cell heterogeneity in enzyme catalytic rates (Davidi et al., 2016; García-Contreras et al., 2012), our model quantitatively illustrates the threshold-analog response (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996) in overflow metabolism (see Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental data with citation support

claims.claim: The cAMP-CRP system plays a crucial role in sensing proteome efficiency and executing the optimal strategy.
claims.source: A growing body of evidence suggests that the cyclic AMP (cAMP)-cAMP receptor protein (CRP) system plays a crucial role in sensing proteome efficiency and executing the optimal strategy (Basan et al., 2015; Towbin et al., 2017; Valgepea et al., 2010; Wehrens et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claims.claim: The cAMP-CRP system alone is insufficient, and additional regulators remain to be identified.
claims.source: However, it has also been suggested that the cAMP-CRP system alone is insufficient, and that additional regulators remain to be identified to fully elucidate this mechanism (Basan et al., 2015; Valgepea et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on regulatory mechanisms

claims.claim: The optimal growth principle in the model can be relaxed to cases where efficient protein allocation is required only for enzymes, rather than ribosomes.
claims.source: Furthermore, since the binary choice between respiration and fermentation is driven by the comparison of proteome efficiencies, the optimal growth principle in our model can be relaxed to the case where efficient protein allocation is required only for enzymes, rather than ribosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical extension of the model

claims.claim: The model remains applicable under suboptimal growth conditions where the inactive portion of ribosomes may vary.
claims.source: This allows our model to remain applicable under suboptimal growth conditions (see Appendix 3.4 for details), where recent experimental studies have shown that the inactive portion of ribosomes (i.e. ribosomes not bound to mRNAs) may vary with culturing conditions (Dai et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018) and between individual cells within the same culture (Pavlou et al., 2025), despite an overall trend toward growth optimization.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies on ribosome activity

claims.claim: In existing rationales, the standard picture of overflow metabolism has primarily been illustrated by a threshold-linear response.
claims.source: In existing rationales (Basan et al., 2015; Chen and Nielsen, 2019; Majewski and Domach, 1990; Shlomi et al., 2011; Varma and Palsson, 1994; Vazquez et al., 2010; Vazquez and Oltvai, 2016), the standard picture of overflow metabolism (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996; Meyer et al., 1984; Nanchen et al., 2006; van Hoek et al., 1998) has primarily been illustrated by a threshold-linear response, which largely relies on the assumption that cells optimize their growth rate for a given rate of carbon influx under each nutrient condition (or similar equivalents; see Appendix 7.3).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to existing modeling approaches

claims.claim: For microbes or tumor cells grown in vitro or in vivo, the given factors are the identity and concentration of the nutrient, rather than the rate of carbon influx.
claims.source: However, in practice, for microbes or tumor cells grown in vitro or in vivo, the given factors are the identity and concentration of the nutrient (Molenaar et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019), rather than the rate of carbon influx.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on growth conditions

claims.claim: The model differs from existing rationales by optimizing cell growth rate purely through protein allocation without imposing a special constraint on carbon influx.
claims.source: Our model resolves this puzzle by significantly differing from existing rationales in its optimization principle, where we optimize cell growth rate purely through protein allocation without imposing a special constraint on carbon influx (see Appendix 7.3 for details).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the model's theoretical approach

claims.claim: Cell heterogeneity is crucial for both explaining the threshold-analog response in overflow metabolism and for resolving the puzzle raised by Shen et al., 2024.
claims.source: More importantly, our model incorporates cell heterogeneity, which is crucial for both explaining the threshold-analog response in overflow metabolism and for resolving this puzzle raised by Shen et al., 2024.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the importance of heterogeneity in the model

claims.claim: In the homogeneous case, cells would not generate fermentation flux if the proteome efficiency in fermentation were lower than in respiration under the optimal growth framework.
claims.source: Furthermore, in this case, cells would not generate fermentation flux if the proteome efficiency in fermentation were lower than that in respiration, under the optimal growth framework.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the homogeneous model

claims.claim: By incorporating heterogeneity in enzyme catalytic rates, the critical growth rate shifts from a single value to a Gaussian distribution across a cell population.
claims.source: By incorporating heterogeneity in enzyme catalytic rates (Davidi et al., 2016; García-Contreras et al., 2012), the critical growth rate (i.e. threshold) shifts from a single value to a Gaussian distribution (see Equation S45 and Appendix 8 for details; see also Appendix 1—figure 4) across a cell population, thereby turning a digital response into the threshold-analog response observed in overflow metabolism (see Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction with citation support

claims.claim: The model results are supported by observed distributions of single-cell growth rates in E. coli.
claims.source: Our model results, based on cell heterogeneity, are further supported by observed distributions of single-cell growth rates in E. coli (Wallden et al., 2016) (see Appendix 1—figure 2B), as well as by experiments involving various types of perturbations (Basan et al., 2015; Holms, 1996; Hui et al., 2015), both in terms of acetate secretion patterns and gene expression in the central metabolic network (see Figures 2—4, Appendix 1—figures 2D and E and 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claims.claim: The heterogeneity patterns predicted by the model are highly consistent with non-genetic heterogeneity observed in single-cell experiments with E. coli and S. cerevisiae.
claims.source: Furthermore, the heterogeneity patterns predicted by our model for fermentation and respiration modes in an isogenic cell population under the same culturing conditions are highly consistent with the non-genetic heterogeneity observed in single-cell experiments with E. coli (Nikolic et al., 2013) and S. cerevisiae (Bagamery et al., 2020), and align with experiments on intra-tumor heterogeneity in glioblastoma (Duraj et al., 2021; Shibao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies on heterogeneity

claims.claim: The model can be broadly applied to address heterogeneity-related challenges in metabolism on a quantitative basis.
claims.source: Finally, our model can be broadly applied to address heterogeneity-related challenges in metabolism on a quantitative basis, including diverse metabolic strategies of cells in various environments (Bagamery et al., 2020; Duraj et al., 2021; Escalante-Chong et al., 2015; Hensley et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2015; Solopova et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the model's broader applicability with citation support

results.result: Overflow metabolism (Warburg effect) is a well-established phenomenon where fast-proliferating cells across bacteria, fungi, and mammalian cells excrete fermentation products despite oxygen availability. Microbes use respiration when nutrients are scarce and aerobic glycolysis when nutrients are abundant.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by extensive citations to established literature (Warburg 1924, Hanahan & Weinberg 2011, Vander Heiden et al. 2009, and multiple studies on bacteria, fungi, and mammalian cells). These are foundational background claims documenting a well-known phenomenon in the field.

results.result: Recent experimental findings contradict prevalent explanations of overflow metabolism. While current theories hold that proteome efficiency in fermentation is consistently higher than respiration, recent measurements show the opposite for many yeast and cancer cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 are supported by appropriate citations. C5 cites Basan et al. 2015 and Chen & Nielsen 2019 for the prevalent explanation, while C6 cites Shen et al. 2024 for contradictory experimental findings. C7 logically follows from comparing these results. This establishes the scientific puzzle the manuscript addresses.

results.result: Most existing explanations of overflow metabolism assume cells optimize growth rate for a given carbon influx rate, but this assumption is questionable since the actual given factors are nutrient identity and concentration. The origin and function of overflow metabolism remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 are supported by multiple citations to existing models and reviews. C8 and C9 appropriately cite studies on optimization assumptions (Molenaar et al. 2009, Scott et al. 2010, Wang et al. 2019), while C10 cites review literature acknowledging the unresolved nature of the problem. This establishes the gap in current understanding.

results.result: Evolutionary pressure drives unicellular organisms to optimize cellular resources for rapid growth through optimal protein allocation corresponding to elementary flux modes. Cancer cells exhibit similar pressures through disruption of growth control and immune evasion.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C15 are well-supported by citations to evolutionary biology and systems biology literature (Scott et al. 2010, Hui et al. 2015, Müller et al. 2014, Hanahan & Weinberg 2011). The connection between microbial optimization and cancer cell behavior (C15) is a reasonable inference supported by the hallmarks of cancer literature.

results.result: The authors propose that overflow metabolism can be understood through optimal protein allocation combined with enzyme catalytic rate heterogeneity. The model quantitatively explains experimental data on E. coli, yeast (Crabtree effect), and cancer cells (Warburg effect).
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 represent the main theoretical contribution. C16 and C17 are supported by the model development throughout the manuscript. C18 is validated by quantitative agreement with E. coli data shown in Figures 1-4. C19 is supported by Figure 5 showing quantitative agreement with yeast and cancer cell data (Bartman et al. 2023, Shen et al. 2024). The model successfully explains previously contradictory observations.

results.result: The authors develop a coarse-grained metabolic model by classifying carbon sources entering upper glycolysis as Group A and organizing biomass precursors into five pools (a1, a2, b, c, d) based on entry points. The coarse-grained model (Figure 1B) is topologically identical to the full metabolic network (Figure 1A).
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 describe the model construction based on established metabolic network topology (Neidhardt et al. 1990, Nelson & Cox 2008). The classification scheme is clearly shown in Figure 1A-B. The topological equivalence (C22) is a direct statement about the model structure that can be verified from the figures.

results.result: The model formulates normalized fluxes as products of proteomic mass fraction and substrate quality (J_i^(N) = φ_i · κ_i). Nutrient quality κ_A varies with nutrient type and concentration for Group A carbon sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C25, and C29 describe the mathematical formulation of the model. These are theoretical definitions that are internally consistent and follow from Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics. The formulation is standard for metabolic modeling and appropriately referenced.

results.result: The model identifies three independent metabolic fates (fermentation, respiration, biomass generation) with distinct proteome fractions. Growth rate is proportional to ribosomal protein fraction, and energy demand is proportional to biomass production rate in bacteria with negligible maintenance energy.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C37 establish key model assumptions supported by appropriate citations. C30-C31 cite Chen & Nielsen 2019 for metabolic fates. C33-C35 cite established cell biology (Neidhardt et al. 1990, Scott et al. 2010, Dai et al. 2017). C36-C37 cite Ebenhöh et al. 2024 and Locasale & Cantley 2010 for energy relationships. These are reasonable simplifying assumptions for bacterial metabolism.

results.result: The model predicts that the choice between respiration and fermentation is determined by comparing proteome efficiencies (ε_r vs ε_f), which are functions of nutrient quality. Under nutrient-poor conditions, respiration is more efficient; under rich conditions, fermentation becomes optimal. A critical nutrient quality κ_A^(C) exists where efficiencies are equal.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C51 present the core theoretical predictions. C39 is established biochemistry (Nelson & Cox 2008). C42-C50 follow logically from the optimization framework and Equation 4. C45 is validated by experimental parameters for E. coli, and C46 is confirmed by Basan et al. 2015 data on lactose. The existence of a critical threshold (C47-C48) follows mathematically from the monotonic increase of Δ(κ_A). This provides a qualitative explanation for aerobic glycolysis (C51).

results.result: In the homogeneous case (all cells identical), optimal protein allocation predicts a digital (step function) response of fermentation flux to growth rate. This is consistent with Molenaar et al. 2009 simulations but incompatible with the threshold-analog response observed experimentally.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 identify a key limitation of the homogeneous model. C52 presents the theoretical prediction (Heaviside step function). C53 correctly notes consistency with Molenaar et al. 2009. C54 identifies the incompatibility with experimental observations (Basan et al. 2015, Holms 1996). This motivates the need for incorporating heterogeneity.

results.result: Cell heterogeneity is ubiquitous in microbes and tumors, with significant metabolic heterogeneity in respiration/fermentation choice. Enzyme k_cat values vary considerably between cells due to varying potassium and phosphate concentrations, creating a distribution (extrinsic noise). The model assumes Gaussian distributions for k_cat values, leading to Gaussian distributions of proteome efficiencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are well-supported by extensive citations to experimental studies on heterogeneity (Ackermann 2015, Bagamery et al. 2020, Nikolic et al. 2013, Davidi et al. 2016, García-Contreras et al. 2012). C60 is an explicit modeling assumption (Gaussian distribution), which is reasonable but simplifying. C61 follows as a mathematical consequence of C60. The Gaussian assumption (C60) is a limitation but is standard practice and validated by agreement with data.

results.result: Incorporating enzyme heterogeneity with 25% CV (equivalent to 12% CV in critical growth rate) transforms the digital response into a threshold-analog response. The model quantitatively agrees with E. coli experimental data for fermentation and respiration fluxes.
results.evaluation: Claims C62 and C64-C67 present the key result resolving the digital vs. analog response problem. C62 is validated by single-cell data from Wallden et al. 2016 (Appendix 1-figure 2B). C64 is a fitting parameter choice (25% CV) that is reasonable given experimental enzyme variability. C65-C66 show quantitative agreement with data in Figures 1C-D (Basan et al. 2015, Holms 1996). C67 summarizes the achievement. The 25% CV is a fitted parameter, but the resulting agreement across multiple datasets supports the model.

results.result: The model successfully predicts the effects of φ_Z perturbation (useless protein overexpression). For each LacZ expression level, fermentation flux shows threshold-analog response to growth rate. Scaling relations and 3D response surfaces quantitatively match experimental data.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 test the model against φ_Z perturbation data. C68 correctly describes the perturbation effect (Basan et al. 2015). C69 and C71-C72 show quantitative agreement with experimental data in Figures 2A-C. The model successfully predicts behavior under this perturbation without additional fitting parameters for the response shape, strengthening confidence in the model.

results.result: The model successfully incorporates energy dissipation (coefficient w) and predicts its effects. A notable characteristic distinguishing energy dissipation from φ_Z perturbation is that fermentation flux increases despite decreasing growth rate at fixed κ_A. Model predictions show good agreement with experimental data.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 test the model against energy dissipation perturbations. C73 describes the model modification. C74 shows agreement with data in Figures 3A-B (Basan et al. 2015). C75 identifies a distinguishing prediction that can be tested. The model successfully handles this perturbation type, further validating the framework.

results.result: The model predictions for translation inhibition are generally consistent with experimental data, though systematic discrepancies arise at low translation rates. Including small maintenance energy (w_0 = 2.5 h^-1) improves agreement, consistent with maintenance energy being typically negligible for bacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 address translation inhibition perturbations. C77 shows general consistency (Appendix 1-figure 2D-E). C78 honestly acknowledges discrepancies at low translation rates. C79 is supported by citations (Basan et al. 2015, Locasale & Cantley 2010). The inclusion of maintenance energy to resolve discrepancies is reasonable and the value (2.5 h^-1) is appropriately small.

results.result: The model successfully predicts distinct behavior for pyruvate (non-Group A carbon source) compared to Group A sources. The critical growth rate λ_C^(py) and fermentation ATP yield β_f^(py) are smaller for pyruvate, resulting in a distinctly different fermentation flux curve validated by experimental data.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 test the model's ability to handle different nutrient types. C81 correctly identifies pyruvate's entry point (Neidhardt et al. 1990, Nelson & Cox 2008). C82 describes the model structure (Figure 3E). C83 presents theoretical predictions about parameter differences. C84 shows validation by experimental data (Holms 1996, Figure 3F). This demonstrates the model's generalizability beyond Group A sources.

results.result: The coarse-grained model predicts enzyme allocation for individual genes in glycolysis and TCA cycle under κ_A perturbation. Glycolysis enzymes show different response patterns than TCA cycle enzymes, which cannot be explained by the C-line response from simplified models. Model predictions overall match experimental data with minor discrepancies attributed to basal expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C93 test enzyme allocation predictions. C85-C87 establish the mapping between model and genes. C88-C89 cite previous C-line models (Hui et al. 2015, You et al. 2013). C90-C91 identify a discrepancy that existing models cannot explain. C92 shows overall agreement with data (Figure 4A-B, Hui et al. 2015). C93 acknowledges minor discrepancies with reasonable explanation. The model successfully predicts differential behavior of glycolysis vs. TCA enzymes.

results.result: For φ_Z perturbation, the model predicts linear responses with all positive slopes for glycolysis and TCA cycle genes, quantitatively matching experimental data. For energy dissipation, φ_4 enzymes show negative slopes, consistent with experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C98 test enzyme allocation under different perturbations. C94-C96 show predictions for φ_Z perturbation match data (Figure 4C-D, Basan et al. 2015) with no fitting parameters (Equations S120-S121). C97-C98 show energy dissipation predictions match experiments (Appendix 1-figure 3K-N). The model successfully predicts enzyme-specific responses to different perturbation types.

results.result: The model extends to yeast and tumors, predicting that proteome efficiencies are increasing functions of nutrient quality, with respiration optimal under poor conditions and fermentation optimal under rich conditions. The standard picture of overflow metabolism has been observed in yeast, though tuning cancer cell growth rates in vivo remains challenging.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 extend the model to eukaryotes. C99-C101 present theoretical predictions (Equations S170-S175). C102 cites experimental validation in yeast (van Hoek et al. 1998). C103 acknowledges experimental limitations for cancer cells. The extension is theoretically sound but relies on similar assumptions as the bacterial model.

results.result: The model resolves the puzzle from Shen et al. 2024 where population-level proteome efficiency in respiration exceeds fermentation despite aerobic glycolysis. By incorporating heterogeneity, the model allows subpopulations to have higher fermentation efficiency even when population average favors respiration. With χ_εr = χ_εf = 0.58, the model quantitatively matches yeast and cancer cell data.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109 address a major contradiction in the field. C104-C105 correctly identify the puzzle from Shen et al. 2024. C106-C108 explain how heterogeneity resolves this: low nutrient quality (C107) plus heterogeneity (C108) allows fermentation in subpopulations despite population-average favoring respiration. C109 shows quantitative agreement with data (Figure 5A-B, Bartman et al. 2023, Shen et al. 2024) using CV = 0.58. The CV value is higher than for E. coli (0.25), which is reasonable given greater heterogeneity in eukaryotes, but is a fitted parameter.

results.result: The model's main findings are that under nutrient-poor conditions, respiration is optimal due to higher proteome efficiency, while in rich media, fermentation becomes optimal as its efficiency increases more rapidly. Combined with heterogeneity, this quantitatively explains the threshold-analog response in overflow metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 summarize the main results. C110-C111 restate the core mechanism with reference to Figure 1E. C112 emphasizes the quantitative agreement with data (Figure 1C, Basan et al. 2015, Holms 1996). These summary claims are well-supported by the detailed results throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The cAMP-CRP system likely plays a role in sensing proteome efficiency and executing optimal strategy, though additional regulators remain to be identified. The model can be relaxed to require efficient allocation only for enzymes (not ribosomes), remaining applicable under suboptimal growth conditions where ribosome activity varies.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 discuss mechanistic implementation and model extensions. C113-C114 appropriately cite evidence for cAMP-CRP involvement (Basan et al. 2015, Towbin et al. 2017) while acknowledging gaps. C115-C116 describe theoretical extensions supported by experimental observations of ribosome variability (Dai et al. 2017, Li et al. 2018, Pavlou et al. 2025). These are reasonable extensions that broaden applicability.

results.result: The model differs from existing rationales by optimizing growth rate through protein allocation without constraining carbon influx, addressing the fact that given factors are nutrient identity and concentration, not influx rate. Cell heterogeneity is crucial for explaining the threshold-analog response and resolving contradictions with Shen et al. 2024.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 contrast the current model with existing approaches. C117 correctly characterizes existing models (Basan et al. 2015, Chen & Nielsen 2019, etc.). C118 cites appropriate references for the critique (Molenaar et al. 2009, Scott et al. 2010). C119 describes the key difference in optimization approach. C120 emphasizes heterogeneity's importance. The distinction from existing models is clearly articulated and justified.

results.result: In the homogeneous case, cells would not ferment if respiration were more efficient. Incorporating enzyme heterogeneity transforms the critical growth rate from a single value to a Gaussian distribution, converting digital to threshold-analog response. The model is supported by single-cell growth rate distributions and heterogeneity patterns in E. coli, yeast, and tumors, and can be broadly applied to metabolism challenges.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C125 discuss the role and validation of heterogeneity. C121 states the homogeneous prediction. C122 explains the transformation mechanism (Equation S45, Appendix 1-figure 4). C123 cites validation by single-cell data (Wallden et al. 2016) and perturbation experiments (Figures 2-4). C124 cites consistency with heterogeneity observations (Nikolic et al. 2013, Bagamery et al. 2020, Duraj et al. 2021). C125 claims broad applicability. The heterogeneity mechanism is well-supported and validated across multiple systems.

results.result: The authors propose that overflow metabolism arises from optimal protein allocation combined with enzyme heterogeneity. The model predicts that proteome efficiency in respiration versus fermentation depends on nutrient quality, with a critical threshold where cells switch from respiration (nutrient-poor) to fermentation (nutrient-rich) as the optimal growth strategy.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers affirm the model's qualitative and quantitative explanatory power. Reviewer 1 states the model 'successfully explain[s] the origins of Overflow Metabolism, both qualitatively and quantitatively' and notes 'This counterintuitive result qualitatively explains Overflow Metabolism.' Reviewer 2 describes the study as 'valuable' and notes the model is 'convincing enough to align with experimental observations.'

results.result: The model incorporates cell heterogeneity in enzyme catalytic rates (modeled as Gaussian distributions) to transform the digital response predicted by homogeneous models into a threshold-analog response. This heterogeneity converts a step-function fermentation flux into the gradual threshold-analog relationship observed experimentally in overflow metabolism.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly affirms this result: 'Quantitative agreement is achieved through the analysis of the heterogeneity of the metabolic status within a cell population. By introducing heterogeneity, the critical growth rate is assumed to follow a Gaussian distribution over the cell population, resulting in accordance with experimental data for E. coli.' Reviewer 2 notes the model 'provides a key aspect on cell-to-cell variability on general metabolic response.'

results.result: The model quantitatively agrees with E. coli experimental data across multiple perturbations including nutrient variation (κA), useless protein expression (φZ), energy dissipation, translation inhibition, and different carbon sources (pyruvate). Model predictions match fermentation/respiration fluxes and enzyme allocation patterns.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 confirms extensive validation: 'The obtained model is extensively tested through perturbations: (1) Introduction of overexpression of useless proteins; (2) Studying energy dissipation; (3) Analysis of the impact of translation inhibition... (4) Alteration of nutrient categories of carbon sources using pyruvate. All model perturbations results are corroborated by E. coli experimental results.' The reviewer notes the model 'aligns well with experimental data, lending credibility to the findings.'

results.result: The model predicts distinct enzyme allocation patterns for glycolysis versus TCA cycle enzymes under different perturbations. Under κA perturbation, glycolysis and TCA enzymes show different responses that cannot be explained by simplified C-line models. Under φZ perturbation, all slopes are positive, while under energy dissipation, TCA enzymes (φ4) show negative slopes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 does not explicitly critique these enzyme allocation predictions, and the overall statement that 'All model perturbations results are corroborated by E. coli experimental results' implicitly includes these findings. The model predictions are stated to match experimental data from Hui et al., 2015 and Basan et al., 2015.

results.result: The model is extended to yeast and cancer cells, providing a quantitative explanation for the Crabtree and Warburg effects. Critically, the model resolves the puzzle that population-level proteome efficiency in respiration exceeds that in fermentation (Shen et al., 2024) by incorporating heterogeneity, allowing subpopulations to favor fermentation even when average efficiency favors respiration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly notes that in the revised version 'the extension of results from bacteria to yeast and cancer is substantiated by a literature base' and that the previous weakness 'has been treated in this current version, where the authors discuss in much more detail and give references supporting this generalization.' Reviewer 1 confirms the model provides quantitative agreement with yeast and cancer data.

results.result: Recent experimental findings (Shen et al., 2024) show that measured proteome efficiency in respiration is higher than in fermentation for many yeast and cancer cells, contradicting prevalent explanations that assume fermentation efficiency is consistently higher.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this experimental finding from the literature. Reviewer 1 acknowledges the model addresses this puzzle, and Reviewer 2's concern about generalization to yeast and cancer was resolved in the revision, implicitly accepting the empirical basis.

results.result: The model's heterogeneity predictions are supported by single-cell growth rate distributions in E. coli and align with observed non-genetic metabolic heterogeneity in E. coli, S. cerevisiae, and tumor cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 confirms the model results are 'in accordance with experimental data for E. coli' and notes consistency with 'observed distributions of single-cell growth rates.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes the model 'provides a key aspect on cell-to-cell variability' though notes 'The potential source of metabolic or proteomic heterogeneity of individual cells remains an open question to be studied.'

results.result: A systematic discrepancy arises in the translation inhibition model when the translation rate is low.
results.evaluation: This limitation is acknowledged in the manuscript but not discussed by reviewers. The claim represents a recognized boundary condition of the model rather than a fundamental challenge to its validity.

results.result: The cAMP-CRP system plays a role in sensing proteome efficiency and executing optimal metabolic strategy, though this system alone is insufficient and additional regulators remain to be identified.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these mechanistic claims, which are supported by literature citations. Reviewer 2 notes 'How individual cells adjust their metabolic strategies also requires future study of the underlying mechanisms,' acknowledging this as an open question rather than a weakness of the current model.

results.result: The model differs from existing approaches by optimizing growth rate through protein allocation without constraining carbon influx, and incorporates cell heterogeneity as crucial for explaining both the threshold-analog response and resolving the Shen et al. puzzle.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 affirms the model's novel approach, stating it 'effectively uses modeling techniques typical of Physics to address complex problems in Biology, demonstrating the potential of interdisciplinary approaches to yield novel insights.' The incorporation of heterogeneity is explicitly validated as achieving 'accordance with experimental data.'

comparisons.comparison: Strong agreement on core theoretical predictions (C42-C51). Both recognize the model qualitatively and quantitatively explains overflow metabolism. OpenEval emphasizes mathematical derivation and validation against E. coli data, while peer reviewers affirm the counterintuitive result and overall explanatory power.

Both address main theoretical contribution (C16-C17) and its validation. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative agreement across multiple organisms (E. coli, yeast, cancer), while peer reviewers confirm the model's qualitative and quantitative explanatory success.

Both address heterogeneity incorporation (C55-C61). OpenEval validates heterogeneity claims with extensive experimental citations and notes Gaussian assumption as reasonable simplification. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm heterogeneity achieves quantitative agreement and provides key insights on cell-to-cell variability.

Both address heterogeneity resolving digital vs. analog response (C62, C64-C67). OpenEval validates with single-cell data and notes 25% CV as fitted but reasonable parameter. Peer reviewers confirm Gaussian distribution approach achieves accordance with E. coli experimental data.

Both address homogeneous model limitation (C52-C54). OpenEval identifies Heaviside prediction as incompatible with experiments, motivating heterogeneity. Peer reviewers implicitly acknowledge this by affirming heterogeneity's necessity for quantitative agreement.

Partial overlap on heterogeneity validation (C122-C124). OpenEval emphasizes transformation mechanism and validation across multiple systems. Peer reviewers confirm cell-to-cell variability importance while noting underlying mechanisms remain open questions.

Both address φ_Z perturbation validation (C68-C72). OpenEval shows quantitative agreement without additional fitting parameters. Peer reviewers confirm all perturbation results are corroborated by E. coli experimental data, lending credibility.

Both address energy dissipation perturbations (C73-C75). OpenEval validates against Basan et al. 2015 data and identifies distinguishing predictions. Peer reviewers include this in overall affirmation that perturbation results align with experimental data.

Both address translation inhibition (C77-C79). OpenEval acknowledges discrepancies at low translation rates and introduces maintenance energy. Peer reviewers include this in general validation statement without specific critique.

Both address nutrient type variation (C81-C84). OpenEval validates pyruvate predictions against Holms 1996 data, demonstrating generalizability. Peer reviewers confirm nutrient category alterations are corroborated by experimental results.

Partial overlap on analog response validation (C66). OpenEval shows quantitative agreement with Basan et al. 2015 and Holms 1996. Peer reviewers confirm model aligns well with experimental data across perturbations.

Strong agreement on enzyme allocation predictions (C85-C93). OpenEval validates differential glycolysis vs. TCA behavior and explains discrepancies existing models cannot address. Peer reviewers implicitly support through general validation statement, though no explicit discussion of these specific predictions.

Strong agreement on enzyme allocation under perturbations (C94-C98). OpenEval emphasizes no-fitting-parameter predictions matching data. Peer reviewers confirm perturbation results are corroborated, implicitly including enzyme-specific responses.

Both address eukaryotic extension (C99-C103). OpenEval presents theoretical predictions with yeast validation but acknowledges cancer cell experimental limitations. Peer reviewers confirm revision substantiated extension with literature base, resolving previous weakness.

Strong agreement on resolving Shen et al. contradiction (C104-C109). OpenEval explains heterogeneity mechanism with CV=0.58 achieving quantitative agreement. Peer reviewers confirm extension to yeast and cancer is now substantiated by literature.
Both address cross-organism validation (C19). OpenEval shows quantitative agreement with yeast and cancer data. Peer reviewers confirm generalization is substantiated in revised version.

Both address contradictory experimental findings (C6-C7). OpenEval cites Shen et al. 2024 contradicting prevalent explanation, establishing scientific puzzle. Peer reviewers implicitly accept empirical basis by acknowledging model addresses this puzzle.

Both address Shen et al. puzzle (C104-C105). OpenEval identifies contradiction between nutrient quality and fermentation observation. Peer reviewers do not challenge this experimental finding and confirm model resolution.

Both address heterogeneity validation (C123-C124). OpenEval cites single-cell data and perturbation experiments supporting heterogeneity role. Peer reviewers confirm accordance with experimental data and cell-to-cell variability importance, noting underlying mechanisms remain open.

Both address translation inhibition discrepancies (C78). OpenEval acknowledges limitation at low translation rates. Peer reviewers mark as uncertain, noting this is recognized boundary condition rather than fundamental challenge.

Both address mechanistic implementation (C113-C114). OpenEval cites cAMP-CRP evidence while acknowledging gaps. Peer reviewers do not challenge these claims, noting underlying mechanisms require future study as open question rather than weakness.

Both address novel optimization approach (C119-C120). OpenEval contrasts with existing models and emphasizes heterogeneity importance. Peer reviewers affirm novel interdisciplinary approach and validate heterogeneity incorporation achieving experimental accordance.
